example.text: El libro está aquí.
example.translation: The book is here.

contexts.explanation: El marks a masculine singular noun here. La is feminine singular; los and las are plural. The article agrees with the noun, not with the speaker.

example.text: Soy de Madrid.
example.translation: I am from Madrid.

contexts.explanation: De introduces a place of origin here. It can also link something to its owner or material; learn its meaning in the whole phrase.

example.text: Quiero té y café.
example.translation: I want tea and coffee.

contexts.explanation: Y adds one item to another: tea and coffee. It does not change for gender or number.

example.text: Estoy en casa.
example.translation: I am at home.

contexts.explanation: En introduces location. In en casa it means “at home”; this expression normally has no article.

example.text: Voy al parque.
example.translation: I am going to the park.

contexts.explanation: A introduces the destination after voy. A and the article el contract to al: voy al parque.

example.text: Tengo un libro.
example.translation: I have a book.

contexts.explanation: Un introduces one unspecified masculine singular thing. Una is the usual feminine form; unos and unas can mean “some.”

example.text: El libro que quiero.
example.translation: The book that I want.

contexts.explanation: Que refers back to el libro and is the object of quiero: the book is what I want. English can omit “that” here; Spanish keeps que.

example.text: Somos de México.
example.translation: We are from Mexico.

contexts.explanation: Somos de México states where we are from. Ser also identifies or classifies people and things. “Permanent versus temporary” is not a reliable rule for choosing ser or estar.

example.text: Ana se lava.
example.translation: Ana washes herself.

contexts.explanation: Ana is both the person washing and the person washed. Se points back to the third-person subject; it does not mean “I know” (sé).

example.text: Creo que Ana viene.
example.translation: I think that Ana is coming.

contexts.explanation: Que introduces what is believed: Ana is coming. Unlike relative que, it does not stand for an earlier noun. English can leave out “that.”

example.text: El libro es suyo.
example.translation: The book is hers.

contexts.explanation: Suyo agrees with the thing owned: libro is masculine singular. It does not tell us the owner’s gender. Here “hers” is one possible interpretation.

example.text: Voy con Ana.
example.translation: I am going with Ana.

contexts.explanation: Con introduces the person accompanying the speaker. Its English meaning here is “with.”

example.text: No entiendo.
example.translation: I do not understand.

contexts.explanation: No goes before entiendo to make the statement negative. Spanish does not add an equivalent of English “do.”

example.text: Camino por el parque.
example.translation: I walk through the park.

contexts.explanation: Por introduces the route taken through the park. Contrast a destination: voy al parque (“I am going to the park”).

example.text: Estudio para aprender.
example.translation: I study in order to learn.

contexts.explanation: Para introduces the goal of studying. Aprender stays in the infinitive after this preposition.

example.text: Lo veo.
example.translation: I see it.

contexts.explanation: Lo stands for the thing seen, such as el libro. “Him” is also possible with a male referent. Here the translation assumes a thing.

example.text: Este libro es bueno.
example.translation: This book is good.

contexts.explanation: Este points out a masculine singular noun near the speaker or currently in focus. Esta, estos and estas agree with other noun forms.

example.text: Como llueve, me quedo en casa.
example.translation: Since it is raining, I am staying at home.

contexts.explanation: At the beginning of this sentence, como introduces the reason for staying home. It means “since” or “because,” not “how?” (cómo).

example.text: Estoy en casa.
example.translation: I am at home.

contexts.explanation: Estoy en casa tells us where the speaker is. Use estar for locations of people and things, even stable ones; ser is used for the location of events.

example.text: Tengo veinte años.
example.translation: I am twenty years old.

contexts.explanation: Spanish expresses age with tener: literally “I have twenty years.” Tengo is its irregular yo present form.

example.text: Voy a estudiar.
example.translation: I am going to study.

contexts.explanation: Voy a estudiar expresses an intention or future action. Voy changes with the subject; estudiar remains an infinitive.

example.text: Le doy un libro.
example.translation: I give her a book.

contexts.explanation: Le identifies the recipient; un libro is what is given. “Her” is chosen for this example, but the context could instead identify him or formal you.

example.text: Este libro es más fácil.
example.translation: This book is easier.

contexts.explanation: Más increases the degree of fácil: the book is easier. It does not change for gender or number.

example.text: Ana me ve.
example.translation: Ana sees me.

contexts.explanation: Me is the person seen. Ana is the subject performing the action. The object pronoun comes before ve.

example.text: Hago la comida.
example.translation: I make the meal.

contexts.explanation: Hago is the irregular yo present form of hacer. The other present forms here use the stem hac-.

example.text: Puedo ir.
example.translation: I can go.

contexts.explanation: Puedo is followed directly by ir, without a preposition. The subject is I; ir stays in the infinitive.

example.text: Ese libro es mío.
example.translation: That book is mine.

contexts.explanation: Ese identifies a masculine singular thing as “that.” Esa, esos and esas agree with other noun forms. Distance can be conversational rather than physical.

example.text: Estudio todos los días.
example.translation: I study every day.

contexts.explanation: Todos agrees with masculine plural días. Todos los días means “every day”; the article stays between todos and días.

example.text: Quiero té o café.
example.translation: I want tea or coffee.

contexts.explanation: O links alternatives. Whether one or both are possible depends on context; the word alone does not always exclude choosing both.

example.text: Quiero ir, pero no puedo.
example.translation: I want to go, but I cannot.

contexts.explanation: Pero introduces an idea that contrasts with the first statement: wanting to go does not mean being able to.

example.text: Él habla español.
example.translation: He speaks Spanish.

contexts.explanation: Él is the subject of habla. Spanish often omits a subject pronoun when the person is clear; including it can clarify or emphasize who acts.

example.text: Quiero otro libro.
example.translation: I want another book.

contexts.explanation: Otro before a singular noun already means “another.” Match its ending to the noun: otro libro, otra casa.

example.text: Digo la verdad.
example.translation: I tell the truth.

contexts.explanation: Digo is the irregular yo present form. Dices, dice and dicen have i in the stem; decimos and decís keep e.

example.text: Un año tiene doce meses.
example.translation: A year has twelve months.

contexts.explanation: Año is masculine: un año, el año. Its regular plural adds s: años.

example.text: Hay un libro aquí.
example.translation: There is a book here.

contexts.explanation: Hay introduces the existence or presence of something. It is the impersonal present form of haber, not a form that changes to agree with the following noun.

example.text: Si llueve, me quedo en casa.
example.translation: If it rains, I stay at home.

contexts.explanation: Si introduces a condition, without a written accent. Here llueve is present indicative, expressing an open condition.

example.text: El libro es mío.
example.translation: The book is mine.

contexts.explanation: Mío agrees with masculine singular libro, not with the owner’s gender. The owner is the speaker.

example.text: Doy un libro.
example.translation: I give a book.

contexts.explanation: Doy is the irregular yo present form of dar. Un libro is what the speaker gives.

example.text: Veo la casa.
example.translation: I see the house.

contexts.explanation: Veo is the yo present form of ver. The English meaning may be “see” or “watch,” depending on the object.

example.text: El libro está sobre la mesa.
example.translation: The book is on the table.

contexts.explanation: Sobre introduces the position on the table in this example. It can also mean “above” without contact; context decides.

example.text: Estudio cuando tengo tiempo.
example.translation: I study when I have time.

contexts.explanation: Cuando introduces the time at which I study. In this habitual statement the verb tengo is in the present indicative.

example.text: Esto es entre tú y yo.
example.translation: This is between you and me.

contexts.explanation: In the ordinary “between” construction, entre takes tú and yo, rather than ti and mí. Learn entre tú y yo as a phrase.

example.text: Yo también estudio español.
example.translation: I also study Spanish.

contexts.explanation: También adds the speaker to other people who study Spanish. Here “also” applies to the statement.

example.text: Ya no vivo aquí.
example.translation: I no longer live here.

contexts.explanation: Ya no says that something was true before and is not true now. Here the speaker no longer lives in the place.

example.text: Ana nos ve.
example.translation: Ana sees us.

contexts.explanation: Nos is the group being seen, including the speaker. Ana performs the action.

example.text: Quiero uno.
example.translation: I want one.

contexts.explanation: Uno stands alone here and means one item; the example assumes a masculine referent such as libro. With a feminine referent, use una.

example.text: Quiero café sin azúcar.
example.translation: I want coffee without sugar.

contexts.explanation: Café sin azúcar is the full noun phrase being requested. Sin azúcar specifies how the coffee is wanted.

example.text: Te veo.
example.translation: I see you.

contexts.explanation: Te is the person seen, addressed informally in the singular. The verb veo identifies the speaker as the subject.

example.text: El libro es muy bueno.
example.translation: The book is very good.

contexts.explanation: Muy increases the degree of bueno. It does not change for gender or number and goes before the adjective or adverb.

example.text: Veo la casa desde aquí.
example.translation: I see the house from here.

contexts.explanation: Desde identifies the point from which the speaker sees the house. Its meaning here is spatial: “from.”

example.text: Sonríe porque sabe qué día es.
example.translation: She smiles because she knows what day it is.

contexts.explanation: porque is used here as a conjunction. Because. Por qué (two words, accented) means why.

contexts.explanation: sabe is a form of saber (present: él / ella / usted). Knowledge or knowing how; compare conocer.

context:n.title: Noun phrase
context:n.text: Read the noun together with its article and modifiers. Articles and adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number; a phrase beginning with de can add information about it.

context:v.title: Verb construction
context:v.text: Read these words together as the action in this sentence. A conjugated verb marks its subject and tense; a dependent infinitive names an action without adding another person ending. Pronouns can accompany a verb.

context:p.title: Connecting phrase
context:p.text: Read this phrase as a unit: it connects the action or description to a place, time, person, purpose, or other complement. The English gloss gives its meaning here; prepositions do not have a single translation in every context.

context:s.title: Reference in context
context:s.text: This expression refers to a person, thing, or idea in the sentence. Relative words connect it to a description; object pronouns and personal a can mark the person affected by an action.

context:c.title: Linking ideas
context:c.text: This word or expression connects the ideas in the sentence. Use its contextual gloss to distinguish meanings such as addition, contrast, cause, and conditions.

context:a.title: Description and agreement
context:a.text: This description belongs to the person or thing described in the sentence. Spanish adjectives normally agree with that noun in gender and number. The noun’s entry shows its gender.

context:r.title: Meaning in context
context:r.text: This expression modifies an action, description, or statement. Its placement and surrounding words determine the intended meaning; the English gloss describes this use.
